chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: Learning chords by ear and note values from Johnny Clark
summary: Smith learned chords and changes by ear on the piano, and banjoist Johnny Clark showed him note values.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: One of the things you said which surprised me a lot was that
Buster Smith - 111
you never really practiced scales or technique much on the saxophone.
No-no-no.
How did you get this sort of speed thing, then?

Well, I think it's mostly... I used to bang around on the piano a little bit. I'd study those chords. I'd try to put as many notes as I could within the chord for a change -- for the chord to change. I'd turn back with something or other, and I'd study those chords, and I'd notice that 7 means one thing, 6 means another thing, diminished means another thing, augmented means another thing.
How did you learn all this? That's quite complicated?
I don't know. It was just by ear! Heh-heh.
No one ever showed you.
No.
No one ever said, 'Hey, Buster, look. I'm going to play a diminished chord now. This means this.'
Mmm-hmm.
No one ever did that?
No. One of the guys showed me the value of a note, when I first tried to learn how to read. He was a banjo player.
Who was that?
A fellow named Johnny Clark. He's in Arizona
Buster Smith - 112
somewhere now.
Was he working with one of the bands?

Mmm-hmm. He was working with Jesse Hooker and them sometimes, downtown there, back in the 20's. He could read, and she showed me the value of the notes and things. Took me out to his home. He'd get off work at night, and we go out there and sit up around 2 or 3 o'clock in the morning. That's why it wasn't long then before I joined the Blue Devils and left here.
